summary: When people ask about surface heat, they often confuse two different Earth-system questions: where the land surface was hottest on average versus where it was warming fastest over time. HeatFlip is a static, zero-login scientific web atlas for "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" built from 38 SHA-256-verified NASA Terra MODIS MOD11C3.061 monthly granules covering April–May 2001–2019 across 25,120 global 1° × 1° land grid cells (~110 km at the Equator). Users explore a 3D globe or search 32,960 places to flip between Hot (mean clear-sky land surface temperature, °C) and Heating (ordinary least squares rate, °C/decade with 95% confidence intervals), then open the Day/Night Detective to test whether nighttime or daytime temperatures changed faster on strictly co-observed 0.05° pixels—separating real trends from statistical uncertainty and cloud-limited gaps.
details:
THE CHALLENGE WE SOLVE

Public climate discussions routinely confuse two different Earth-system questions: where the land surface was hottest on average versus where it was heating fastest over time. People also misread noisy confidence intervals crossing zero as "no change," or compare daytime and nighttime trends from different clear-sky days—confusing cloud shifts with real diurnal change.

WHAT HEATFLIP DOES

HeatFlip is a zero-login orbital web atlas built from 38 SHA-256-verified NASA Terra MODIS (MOD11C3.061) monthly granules covering April–May 2001–2019 across 25,120 global 1° × 1° WGS84 land cells (~110 km at the Equator):

1. Explore (Hot vs. Heating): Spin the 3D WebGL globe (or automatic 2D fallback), search 32,960 GeoNames places, or enter exact coordinates to flip between Surface Heat (mean °C) and Heating Rate (ordinary least squares °C/decade with two-sided 95% t-intervals), compare any two cells A vs. B, and export provenance-rich CSVs.

2. Day/Night Detective: Restricts every cell-month strictly to co-observed 0.05° pixels passing MODIS C6.1 QC at both ~10:30 (Day) and ~22:30 (Night) local solar time (222.25M paired pixel-months) and fits yearly Night minus Day directly by OLS.

VERIFIED FINDINGS (APRIL–MAY 2001–2019)

- Hotter is not always heating faster: Faisalabad's 1° cell (r121c253) averaged an intense 36.98 °C by day, yet its 19-year trend is unresolved (-0.30 °C/decade, 95% CI -1.39 to +0.80: Direction uncertain). Cooler Cairo (r120c211, 34.49 °C mean) warmed clearly at +1.02 °C/decade by day (95% CI +0.34 to +1.70) and +1.31 °C/decade by night.

- Matched diurnal divergence: Istanbul (r131c208) saw Night outpace Day (+0.93 °C/decade, 95% CI +0.04 to +1.81), whereas Montreal (r135c106) saw Day outpace Night (-1.29 °C/decade, 95% CI -2.13 to -0.46), yielding a formal A-minus-B contrast of -2.13 °C/decade across 15 common years.

- Global accounting: 13,424 Day, 12,187 Night, and 9,791 Paired cells pass our >=15-of-19-year & endpoint gates; sparser cloudy cells remain null (Insufficient observations, never 0).

HOW WE BUILT IT & SCIENTIFIC BOUNDARIES

Built with Python (pyhdf, NumPy, SciPy), TypeScript, React 19, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Apache ECharts, Fuse.js, Zod, Vitest, and Playwright (cross-checked to <0.0001 °C against raw-HDF4 SciPy runs). Published strictly for April–May 2001–2019 (ending in 2019 avoids post-2020 Terra orbital-drift solar-time aliasing; annual 228-month mode not built). Clear-sky ~110 km skin temperature is not 2 m weather-station air temperature, daily min/max, thermal comfort, causal attribution, or a future forecast.
